title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
summary: Keep a min-heap of the k largest values seen so far. Push each number; if the heap grows past k, pop its smallest. At the end the heap's top is the k-th largest.

complexity.note: Quickselect is O(n) on average, O(n²) worst case.

intuition: The k-th largest is the smallest of the top k values.
A min-heap of size k keeps exactly those top k, smallest on top.
When a 6th value arrives for k = 5, the smallest of the six can't be in the top 5: pop it.
pitfalls: Using a max-heap of all n values is O(n log n) and O(n) space.
Sorting is O(n log n); fine to mention, but the heap or quickselect is expected.

title: Last Stone Weight
summary: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones: equal stones both vanish, otherwise the difference goes back. A max-heap always gives the two heaviest in O(log n).

complexity.note: Each smash removes at least one stone.

intuition: Each round needs the two largest values: exactly what a max-heap provides.
Push back `y - x` only when it's non-zero.
Return the last stone, or 0 if none are left.
pitfalls: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap; pass `Collections.reverseOrder()`.
Re-sorting the array each round is O(n² log n).

title: K Closest Points to Origin
summary: Keep the k closest points in a max-heap keyed by squared distance. When the heap grows past k, drop the farthest. What remains are the k closest.

complexity.note: Compare squared distances; no square roots needed.

intuition: To keep the k smallest, use a max-heap and evict its top.
`x² + y²` preserves the distance order without `Math.sqrt`.
Output order doesn't matter.
pitfalls: Using sqrt and doubles: slower and introduces rounding.
Comparator overflow with `a - b` style comparisons on large values; use Integer.compare.

title: Task Scheduler
summary: Tasks of the same type need `n` idle slots between them. The most frequent task decides the shape: it creates `maxFreq - 1` gaps of size `n`. Fill them with other tasks; if there are more tasks than slots, no idling is needed and the answer is the task count.

complexity.note: Counting 26 letters; the formula is O(1) after that.

intuition: Lay out the most frequent task with n slots after each: `(maxFreq - 1) × (n + 1)` frames.
Tasks tied for the max frequency fill the final frame: add `countMax`.
If tasks outnumber the frames, there are no idle slots: answer is `tasks.length`.
pitfalls: Counting only one task with the maximum frequency.
A max-heap simulation also works and is good to explain; the formula is faster.
input: tasks = [A, A, A, B, B, B], n = 2

steps.title: Count the tasks
steps.explain: The most frequent task appears 3 times; 2 task type(s) share that count.

steps.title: Build the frames
steps.explain: (3 − 1) × (2 + 1) + 2 = 8 slots, including idles.

steps.title: Answer
steps.explain: All tasks fit in the frames; idle slots are needed.

title: Top K Frequent Words
summary: Return the k most frequent words, ties broken alphabetically. Count words, then keep a size-k min-heap whose "smallest" is the least frequent word (and, among equal counts, the alphabetically last). Pop everything and reverse.
intuition: The heap's top must be the word that should be evicted first.
Evict lower counts first; for equal counts, evict the alphabetically larger word.
Popping gives worst-to-best, so reverse at the end.
pitfalls: Getting the tie-break backwards in the min-heap comparator.
Forgetting to reverse the popped order.

title: Reorganize String
summary: Rearrange letters so no two neighbours are equal. Greedily place the most frequent remaining letter, but never the one just placed: pop the top two letters from a max-heap, append both, and push them back with one fewer count.

complexity.note: The heap holds at most 26 letters.

intuition: If any letter appears more than `(n + 1) / 2` times, it's impossible.
Placing the two most frequent letters together each round keeps them from bunching up later.
When only one letter is left, it must have count 1.
pitfalls: Placing the most frequent letter twice in a row.
Missing the impossibility check, then producing an invalid string.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
summary: Keep the smaller half of the numbers in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap, balanced so the max-heap has the same size or one more. The median is the max-heap's top, or the average of both tops.

complexity.note: addNum is O(log n); findMedian is O(1).

intuition: `low` (max-heap) holds the smaller half; `high` (min-heap) holds the larger half.
Every value in `low` is ≤ every value in `high`.
Add to `low`, move its top to `high`, then move back if `high` got bigger.
Odd count: median is `low.peek()`. Even: average the two tops.
pitfalls: Letting the heaps drift more than one apart.
Sorting on every add is O(n log n) per call.
